title: 4  Data Wrangling I - Loading, Cleaning and Tidying
text:
4.5 dplyr
The purpose of dplyr is to transform and summarise data frames in a readable, consistent way. As with git it consists of core verbs that are intended to be human-readable, e.g.

mutate() - add or transform columns
select() - subset columns
filter() - subset rows
summarise() - reduces multiple values down to a single summary
arrange() - reorder rows

As an example, consider the gapminder dataset. This provides country-level data on life expectancy, GDP per capita and population, over time.

library(tidyverse)
library(gapminder)
gapminder

# A tibble: 1,704 × 6
   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
 4 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
 5 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
 6 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.
 7 Afghanistan Asia       1982    39.9 12881816      978.
 8 Afghanistan Asia       1987    40.8 13867957      852.
 9 Afghanistan Asia       1992    41.7 16317921      649.
10 Afghanistan Asia       1997    41.8 22227415      635.
# ℹ 1,694 more rows


As we can see, the gapminder is an r tibble, with 1704 rows and 6 columns. Suppose we want to compute the average GDP and life expectancy of countries in Asia in 2007. Here’s an example using dplyr to accomplish this.

gapminder |> 
    filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia") |>
    mutate(gdp_billions = gdpPercap * pop / 1e9) |>
    arrange(desc(lifeExp)) |>
    select(country, lifeExp, gdp_billions) |>
    summarise(mean_life_expectancy=mean(lifeExp), mean_gdp=mean(gdp_billions))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_life_expectancy mean_gdp
                 <dbl>    <dbl>
1                 70.7     628.


The code above is human readable - each row describes an operation applied to the dataset, chained together with pipes |>. In other words, we can look at the code and see that we

Took the gapminder dataset,
Applied a filter to the year and continent,
Added a computed column (gdp_billions),
Ordered by lifeExp,
Selected the relevant columns.
Used summarise to compute the mean of both life expectancy and GDP.







TipOther Summarise Functions



summarise works with most of the functions you would expect, including things like mean, median, sum, min, max. We can also count the number of rows using n() and the number of unique values with n_distinct().


If we choose any pipe |> and delete the pipe and everything after it, we still get a tibble output which just applies the subset of operations before the pipe. We can thus interpret the pipes as “chaining together” the operations we want to apply.
Note that this can have an impact on cost. For example, consider this example:

gapminder |> 
    mutate(gdp_billions = gdpPercap * pop / 1e9) |>
    arrange(desc(lifeExp)) |>
    filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia") |>
    select(country, lifeExp, gdp_billions)

# A tibble: 33 × 3
   country          lifeExp gdp_billions
   <fct>              <dbl>        <dbl>
 1 Japan               82.6       4035. 
 2 Hong Kong, China    82.2        277. 
 3 Israel              80.7        164. 
 4 Singapore           80.0        215. 
 5 Korea, Rep.         78.6       1145. 
 6 Taiwan              78.4        666. 
 7 Kuwait              77.6        119. 
 8 Oman                75.6         71.5
 9 Bahrain             75.6         21.1
10 Vietnam             74.2        208. 
# ℹ 23 more rows


The output is the same, but because we apply the mutate operation before the filter, we will compute gdp_billions for all 1704 rows before discarding all but 23 rows. This is wasteful, and can have a significant performance implication on larger datasets!

4.5.1 Grouping
Grouping data is a powerful feature in dplyr that allows you to perform operations within subsets of your data. The group_by() function is used to specify one or more variables to group by, and then you can apply summary functions or transformations to each group.
For example, suppose we want to compute the average life expectancy for each continent in the gapminder dataset. We can first group by the continent:

grouped = gapminder |>
    group_by(continent)
grouped

# A tibble: 1,704 × 6
# Groups:   continent [5]
   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
 4 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
 5 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
 6 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.
 7 Afghanistan Asia       1982    39.9 12881816      978.
 8 Afghanistan Asia       1987    40.8 13867957      852.
 9 Afghanistan Asia       1992    41.7 16317921      649.
10 Afghanistan Asia       1997    41.8 22227415      635.
# ℹ 1,694 more rows


The result tells us that we have a tibble that has been separated into subgroups, and shows the first of the groups. We can access other groups as follows:

group_keys(grouped) # view what groups are available

# A tibble: 5 × 1
  continent
  <fct>    
1 Africa   
2 Americas 
3 Asia     
4 Europe   
5 Oceania  

group_split(grouped)[[5]] # access the Oceania group

# A tibble: 24 × 6
   country   continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
   <fct>     <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
 1 Australia Oceania    1952    69.1  8691212    10040.
 2 Australia Oceania    1957    70.3  9712569    10950.
 3 Australia Oceania    1962    70.9 10794968    12217.
 4 Australia Oceania    1967    71.1 11872264    14526.
 5 Australia Oceania    1972    71.9 13177000    16789.
 6 Australia Oceania    1977    73.5 14074100    18334.
 7 Australia Oceania    1982    74.7 15184200    19477.
 8 Australia Oceania    1987    76.3 16257249    21889.
 9 Australia Oceania    1992    77.6 17481977    23425.
10 Australia Oceania    1997    78.8 18565243    26998.
# ℹ 14 more rows


Far more useful, though, is to use the summarise command to aggregate the groups directly, producing a new tibble with the results. The below command does this:

gapminder |>
    group_by(continent) |>
    summarise(avg_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  continent avg_lifeExp
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Africa           48.9
2 Americas         64.7
3 Asia             60.1
4 Europe           71.9
5 Oceania          74.3








TipCounting with count()



A very common task is simply to count how many rows fall into each group. Doing this with group_by and summarise(n = n()) works, but it is so common that dplyr provides a shorthand, count():

gapminder |>
    filter(year == 2007) |>
    count(continent)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  continent     n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Africa       52
2 Americas     25
3 Asia         33
4 Europe       30
5 Oceania       2


This is exactly equivalent to group_by(continent) |> summarise(n = n()), but much more concise.








ImportantGrouping by several variables



When we group by more than one variable, summarise only removes the last grouping variable, so the result is still grouped by the others. dplyr prints a message to warn us about this:

gapminder |>
    group_by(continent, year) |>
    summarise(avg_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp))

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by continent and year.
ℹ Output is grouped by continent.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(continent, year))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.


# A tibble: 60 × 3
# Groups:   continent [5]
   continent  year avg_lifeExp
   <fct>     <int>       <dbl>
 1 Africa     1952        39.1
 2 Africa     1957        41.3
 3 Africa     1962        43.3
 4 Africa     1967        45.3
 5 Africa     1972        47.5
 6 Africa     1977        49.6
 7 Africa     1982        51.6
 8 Africa     1987        53.3
 9 Africa     1992        53.6
10 Africa     1997        53.6
# ℹ 50 more rows


The output is still grouped by continent, and any later operations (e.g. another summarise or mutate) will be applied within each continent, which is often not what we intended. To return an ungrouped tibble, and silence the message, pass .groups = "drop" to summarise:

gapminder |>
    group_by(continent, year) |>
    summarise(avg_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 60 × 3
   continent  year avg_lifeExp
   <fct>     <int>       <dbl>
 1 Africa     1952        39.1
 2 Africa     1957        41.3
 3 Africa     1962        43.3
 4 Africa     1967        45.3
 5 Africa     1972        47.5
 6 Africa     1977        49.6
 7 Africa     1982        51.6
 8 Africa     1987        53.3
 9 Africa     1992        53.6
10 Africa     1997        53.6
# ℹ 50 more rows


Alternatively, ungroup() removes all grouping from a tibble at any point in a pipeline.

title: 4  Data Wrangling I - Loading, Cleaning and Tidying
text:
4.6 tidyr
The gapminder dataset is a tall dataset; it contains multiple rows for each country and continent. tidyr contains pivot operations to allow us to convert tall datasets into wide datasets, for example:

gapminder_wide = gapminder |> 
    select(country, year, lifeExp) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from=year, values_from=lifeExp)
gapminder_wide

# A tibble: 142 × 13
   country `1952` `1957` `1962` `1967` `1972` `1977` `1982` `1987` `1992` `1997`
   <fct>    <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
 1 Afghan…   28.8   30.3   32.0   34.0   36.1   38.4   39.9   40.8   41.7   41.8

# ℹ 132 more rows
# ℹ 2 more variables: `2002` <dbl>, `2007` <dbl>


Now we end up with a 142 \(\times\) 13 tibble whose entries are lifeExp. We can use the “wide” dataset to easily calculate the change in life expecancy:

gapminder_wide |>
    mutate(change = `2007` - `1952`) |>
    select(country, change)

# A tibble: 142 × 2
   country     change
   <fct>        <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan   15.0
 2 Albania       21.2
 3 Algeria       29.2
 4 Angola        12.7
 5 Argentina     12.8
 6 Australia     12.1
 7 Austria       13.0
 8 Bahrain       24.7
 9 Bangladesh    26.6
10 Belgium       11.4
# ℹ 132 more rows








Tip



The backquotes, above, (around 2007 and 1952) are needed to tell R that these are not to be treated as numbers but as literal column names. They would also be needed if for column names containing spaces or symbols like + or $.


The “inverse” of pivot_wider is pivot_longer. Here we need to tell it which columns to gather up: every column except country. Rather than listing them all by hand, we can use the tidyselect helper syntax -country, which means “all columns except country”:

gapminder_wide |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -country,
        names_to = "year",
        values_to = "lifeExp"
    )

# A tibble: 1,704 × 3
   country     year  lifeExp
   <fct>       <chr>   <dbl>
 1 Afghanistan 1952     28.8
 2 Afghanistan 1957     30.3
 3 Afghanistan 1962     32.0
 4 Afghanistan 1967     34.0
 5 Afghanistan 1972     36.1
 6 Afghanistan 1977     38.4
 7 Afghanistan 1982     39.9
 8 Afghanistan 1987     40.8
 9 Afghanistan 1992     41.7
10 Afghanistan 1997     41.8
# ℹ 1,694 more rows








TipSelecting columns



The cols = -country syntax above is an example of tidyselect, a mini-language for choosing columns that also works in select(). Other useful helpers include starts_with("x"), ends_with("x"), contains("x") and where(is.numeric). These are much more robust than listing column positions by number, since they keep working even if the columns are reordered.



4.6.1 Separating Columns
Pivoting fixes datasets where a variable is spread across many columns (like the years above) or across many rows (like table2 in the tidy-data example). It does not, however, fix table3, where a single cell holds two values at once:
table3
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   country      year rate
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 Afghanistan  1999 745/19987071
#> 2 Afghanistan  2000 2666/20595360
#> 3 Brazil       1999 37737/172006362
#> 4 Brazil       2000 80488/174504898
#> 5 China        1999 212258/1272915272
#> 6 China        2000 213766/1280428583
The rate column packs cases and population into one string separated by a /, which violates the tidy-data rule that each cell contains a single value. To tidy it we need to split the column, which is the job of separate_wider_delim from tidyr. We tell it which column to split, the delimiter to split on, and the names of the new columns:

table3 |>
    separate_wider_delim(rate, delim = "/", names = c("cases", "population"))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  country      year cases  population
  <chr>       <dbl> <chr>  <chr>     
1 Afghanistan  1999 745    19987071  
2 Afghanistan  2000 2666   20595360  
3 Brazil       1999 37737  172006362 
4 Brazil       2000 80488  174504898 
5 China        1999 212258 1272915272
6 China        2000 213766 1280428583


Notice that the new cases and population columns are of type <chr> (text), because they were extracted from a string. If we want to do arithmetic with them we must convert them to numbers, for example with mutate and as.integer:

table3 |>
    separate_wider_delim(rate, delim = "/", names = c("cases", "population")) |>
    mutate(cases = as.integer(cases), population = as.integer(population))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  country      year  cases population
  <chr>       <dbl>  <int>      <int>
1 Afghanistan  1999    745   19987071
2 Afghanistan  2000   2666   20595360
3 Brazil       1999  37737  172006362
4 Brazil       2000  80488  174504898
5 China        1999 212258 1272915272
6 China        2000 213766 1280428583


With table3 split apart and converted, the data is finally tidy and ready for analysis.






Tip



separate_wider_delim splits on a fixed delimiter, but its siblings handle other cases: separate_wider_position splits at fixed character widths (useful for fixed-width codes), and separate_wider_regex splits using a regular expression for more complex patterns. There is also a separate_longer_delim, which puts each piece on its own row rather than in its own column.

text:
5.1 Joins: Connecting Multiple Tables
A join combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them. There are various types of joins depending on what kinds of data you want to join; we’ll go through each of them. To illustrate we will use the (synthetic) student data from student_data.csv and student_grades.csv.

library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

student_data = read_csv("data/student_data.csv")
student_grades = read_csv("data/student_grades.csv")
head(student_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
     ID `Given Name` `Family Name` `Date of Birth`
  <dbl> <chr>        <chr>                   <dbl>
1     1 Adaora       Nkomo                   37205
2     2 Hiroshi      Tanaka                  37845
3     3 Aaliyah      Williams                37505
4     4 Dimitri      Volkov                  37717
5     5 Amara        Baptiste                37387
6     6 Rajesh       Krishnamurthy           38218

head(student_grades)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  `Student ID` Course   Grade
         <dbl> <chr>    <dbl>
1            1 MATH6195    68
2            2 MATH6195    67
3            3 MATH6195    68
4            4 MATH6195    74
5            5 MATH6195    52
6            6 MATH6195    85


We have two tables, and they are linked by a common ID column (called Student ID in student_grades). Names and dates of birth are available in student_data but the student grades are in student_grades. Each student takes multiple courses, so the relationship between the student and grade tables is one-to-many.






TipWhy Store Data Like This?



Storing in multiple tables is good practice for multiple reasons:

Data size: If we stored it in a single flat table, the student name would be repeated for every course they take. This can make the data files significantly larger!
Consistency and Integrity: If a student changes their name, it only needs to be updated in one place.
Flexibilty: Adding new attributes is much easier. For example, if we wanted to start recording student reference requests, we could add a new student_references table, with a one-to-many relationship with student_data but no link at all to student_grades.
Clarity: It’s easier to think about the data structure if it is logically separated like this (e.g. “each student takes multiple courses”).




5.1.1 Cleaning Column Names
Before we go further, notice that these column names are awkward to work with: some contain spaces (Student ID, Date of Birth) and the capitalisation is inconsistent. Every time we refer to such a name we have to wrap it in backticks — for example student_grades$`Student ID` — which is easy to forget and clutters our code.
The clean_names function from the janitor package fixes this in a single step, converting every column name to a consistent snake_case style with no spaces or capitals. We will clean both tables now and keep the tidied versions, so that the rest of this chapter can refer to columns without backticks:

library(janitor)
student_data = clean_names(student_data)
student_grades = clean_names(student_grades)
names(student_data)

[1] "id"            "given_name"    "family_name"   "date_of_birth"

names(student_grades)

[1] "student_id" "course"     "grade"     


So Given Name becomes given_name, Date of Birth becomes date_of_birth, and the two columns that link the tables are now id (in student_data) and student_id (in student_grades). Cleaning names up front like this is often the very first thing worth doing when you load a messy dataset, and it is a good habit to get into.


5.1.2 Inner Join
An inner join takes two tables and joins them together into a single table on based on the matching column, returning only rows that exist in both tables.

result = inner_join(student_data, student_grades, by=c("id" = "student_id"))
head(result)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
     id given_name family_name date_of_birth course   grade
  <dbl> <chr>      <chr>               <dbl> <chr>    <dbl>
1     1 Adaora     Nkomo               37205 MATH6195    68
2     1 Adaora     Nkomo               37205 MATH2010    59
3     1 Adaora     Nkomo               37205 MATH2011    58
4     2 Hiroshi    Tanaka              37845 MATH6195    67
5     2 Hiroshi    Tanaka              37845 MATH2010    72
6     2 Hiroshi    Tanaka              37845 MATH2011    72


Notice how the result contains the columns from both tables. The column we joined on appears only once (as id, its name in the left table), rather than being duplicated as both id and student_id.






Tipby = c(...) and join_by()



The by = c("id" = "student_id") syntax says “match the id column in the left table to the student_id column in the right table”. Recent versions of dplyr provide a newer, more flexible alternative called join_by(), which you will increasingly see in documentation and online:
inner_join(student_data, student_grades, join_by(id == student_id))
Both forms do the same thing here. join_by() uses == (rather than a named string), and can also express more advanced matches such as joining on inequalities. We will use the by = c(...) form in these notes, but the two are interchangeable for our purposes.


Let’s look at the rows.

nrow(result)

[1] 53

nrow(student_grades)

[1] 59


See result has fewer rows than student_grades. This must mean there are some student IDs in the student_grades table that are not in the student_data table. Let’s check:

setdiff(student_grades$student_id, student_data$id)

[1] 21 22


There are two missing students from student_data. Because this is an inner join these were excluded from the final table. Let’s now check if there are any students in student_data that are not present in the result.

setdiff(student_data$id, result$id)

[1] 7


It seems the student with ID 7 is missing:

result |>
    filter(id == 7)

# A tibble: 0 × 6
# ℹ 6 variables: id <dbl>, given_name <chr>, family_name <chr>,
#   date_of_birth <dbl>, course <chr>, grade <dbl>


To check why this might be, we can look for that student in the student_grades table:

student_grades |>
    filter(student_id == 7)

# A tibble: 0 × 3
# ℹ 3 variables: student_id <dbl>, course <chr>, grade <dbl>


So the student is missing because they have no grade records, so the inner join excludes them from the final table. Hopefully they have applied for special considerations!


5.1.3 Left / Right Join
Left and right join keep all the records in the left table or the right table, respectively, in the join statement. Let’s see what the result looks like with a left join instead:

result = left_join(student_data, student_grades, by=c("id" = "student_id"))
result |> filter(id == 7)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
     id given_name family_name date_of_birth course grade
  <dbl> <chr>      <chr>               <dbl> <chr>  <dbl>
1     7 Lin        Yifan               38146 <NA>      NA


Now the student who has no student_grades records is still present in the final table. However, because there are no grade records, the table is filled with <NA> under course and grade. Right join is essentially the same, but keeps records in the right table.


5.1.4 Outer Join
Outer join keeps records in both tables. In dplyr this is called a full_join; this matches SQL’s FULL OUTER JOIN (see Week 7), which is often shortened to just “full join”.

result = full_join(student_data, student_grades, by=c("id" = "student_id"))
result |> filter(id == 7)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
     id given_name family_name date_of_birth course grade
  <dbl> <chr>      <chr>               <dbl> <chr>  <dbl>
1     7 Lin        Yifan               38146 <NA>      NA


We see that the result contains the student with missing grades, but it will also contain the two students who were missing in the student_data table:

result |> filter(id %in% c(21,22))

# A tibble: 6 × 6
     id given_name family_name date_of_birth course   grade
  <dbl> <chr>      <chr>               <dbl> <chr>    <dbl>
1    21 <NA>       <NA>                   NA MATH6195    70
2    22 <NA>       <NA>                   NA MATH6195    89
3    21 <NA>       <NA>                   NA MATH2010    71
4    22 <NA>       <NA>                   NA MATH2010    56
5    21 <NA>       <NA>                   NA MATH2011    62
6    22 <NA>       <NA>                   NA MATH2011    84


Now the given_name, family_name and date_of_birth fields are all <NA>.


5.1.5 Other Types of Join
There are some other types of join which are much less common to encounter. Here are some examples:

semi_join(x, y, by="id"): keeps rows in x that have a match in y but does not add columns from y.
anti_join(x, y, by="id"): keeps rows in x that do not have a match in y, but again does not add columns from y.
cross_join(x,y): gives the cartesian product of x and y, that is, the tibbles are not matched on any common column, but rather all possible combinations of rows in x and y appear.







WarningTwo common surprises when joining



Duplicated column names. If both tables contain a (non-key) column with the same name — say both have a notes column — the join cannot keep them both under one name. By default dplyr disambiguates them by adding the suffixes .x (from the left table) and .y (from the right), giving notes.x and notes.y. You can control these with the suffix argument.
Many-to-many joins. Our student example is one-to-many: each student has many grades, but each grade belongs to one student. If instead both tables have several matching rows for a key (a many-to-many relationship), the join produces a row for every combination of matches, which can multiply the number of rows dramatically. Recent versions of dplyr will warn you when this happens, as it is very often a sign of a mistake in the join.

5.2 Strings
We often need to deal with purely textual data in data science. While it would be nice for all the data we receive to be highly structured, we frequently get “free text” input from users, where the input may need to be cleaned or otherwise processed before it can be used. In tidyverse this is the role of the stringr library, which provides a large family of functions (all prefixed with str_) that are designed to work nicely with the tibble format.
A key feature of every stringr function is that it is vectorised: it works on a single string or on a whole vector (or column) of strings, which is exactly what we need when cleaning a column of a data frame.

str_length("Hello World")

[1] 11

str_length(c("Alice", "Bob", "Dave"))

[1] 5 3 4


To illustrate the main operations we will use a small vector of deliberately messy names, of the kind you might get from a free-text form:

messy_names <- c("  Alice  ", "BOB", "cara-mae", "  dave ")


5.2.1 Measuring and Extracting
str_length returns the number of characters, and str_sub extracts a substring between two positions. Positions count from 1, and negative positions count from the end of the string:

str_sub("MATH6195", 1, 4)   # first four characters

[1] "MATH"

str_sub("MATH6195", -4, -1) # last four characters

[1] "6195"




5.2.2 Standardising Case
Inconsistent capitalisation is one of the most common problems in free text. str_to_lower, str_to_upper and str_to_title standardise it:

str_to_lower(messy_names)

[1] "  alice  " "bob"       "cara-mae"  "  dave "  

str_to_title(messy_names)

[1] "  Alice  " "Bob"       "Cara-Mae"  "  Dave "  




5.2.3 Trimming Whitespace
Stray spaces are another frequent nuisance, and they are easy to miss because they are invisible. str_trim removes leading and trailing whitespace, while str_squish also collapses repeated internal spaces down to a single space:

str_trim(messy_names)

[1] "Alice"    "BOB"      "cara-mae" "dave"    

str_squish("  too    many   spaces ")

[1] "too many spaces"




5.2.4 Detecting and Matching
str_detect tests whether each string contains a pattern, returning a logical vector — which makes it ideal for use inside filter(). str_starts and str_ends are convenient special cases for the beginning and end of a string:

str_detect(messy_names, "a")   # which names contain a lower-case "a"?

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE

str_starts(messy_names, "B")

[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE


Note that matching is case-sensitive: "Alice" does not match "a" because it contains an upper-case "A". A common pattern is therefore to standardise case with str_to_lower before matching.


5.2.5 Replacing and Removing
str_replace replaces the first match of a pattern, str_replace_all replaces every match, and str_remove / str_remove_all delete matches entirely:

str_replace("cara-mae", "-", " ")      # first match only

[1] "cara mae"

str_replace_all("a-b-c-d", "-", "_")   # every match

[1] "a_b_c_d"

str_remove("MATH6195", "MATH")

[1] "6195"




5.2.6 Splitting and Combining
str_split breaks a string into pieces on a separator. It returns a list, because each input string might split into a different number of pieces:

str_split("MATH6195,MATH6196,MATH6197", ",")

[[1]]
[1] "MATH6195" "MATH6196" "MATH6197"


Going the other way, str_c joins strings together — either element-wise (like the base-R function paste0, which we met in Week 2), or into a single string using the collapse argument:

str_c("MATH", 6195)                  # element-wise; numbers are coerced to text

[1] "MATH6195"

str_c(messy_names, collapse = ", ")  # collapse a vector into one string

[1] "  Alice  , BOB, cara-mae,   dave "




5.2.7 Putting It Together
Because these functions are vectorised, they slot directly into a dplyr pipeline. Here we clean a whole column of raw names in a single mutate, squishing out stray whitespace and standardising the case:

tibble(raw = messy_names) |>
    mutate(clean = str_to_title(str_squish(raw)))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  raw         clean   
  <chr>       <chr>   
1 "  Alice  " Alice   
2 "BOB"       Bob     
3 "cara-mae"  Cara-Mae
4 "  dave "   Dave    








TipRegular Expressions



The pattern argument to functions like str_detect, str_replace and str_split is not just plain text: it is interpreted as a regular expression. A regular expression is a “mini language” that allows you to describe flexible patterns to search for, such as “a run of digits” or “an @ surrounded by letters” — which is how you would detect phone numbers or email addresses entered into a free-text box. The simple patterns we used above ("a", "-", ",") happen to be literal text, so they behave as you would expect; but be aware that some characters (such as ., * and ?) have special meanings. We won’t cover regular expressions in detail in this course, but they are well worth knowing about. A good resource for learning is regex101.

5.3 Dates
When we imported the student data above, there was a column — now called date_of_birth after cleaning — that did not appear to contain dates:

student_data$date_of_birth

 [1] 37205 37845 37505 37717 37387 38218 38146 37596 38167 37590 37472 37803
[13] 37283 37852 37900 37865 38162 37870 37282 37481

typeof(student_data$date_of_birth[1])

[1] "double"


The numbers above are Excel format dates. They are the number of days that have elapsed since Excel’s “day zero”, which is December 30, 1899. In theory we could process these dates using this knowledge, but it is much more convenient to convert the number to a proper date type in R. This (and more) functionality is provided by lubridate, a package in tidyverse.

5.3.1 Loading and Converting Dates
Loading dates is surprisingly complex because there is no standard format. For example, here are a variety of perfectly valid ways to represent the date “11th August 2025”:

dates = c(
    '2025-08-11',
    '11/08/2025',
    '08/11/2025',
    '11 August, 2025',
    '11-Aug-2025'
)

The list above is non-exhaustive, so some domain knowledge will always be required to load dates. R may try to infer a date format, but it might be wrong. It is always safer to specify the date format, or at least, to carefully check that dates have been loaded correctly before doing any data analysis.
lubridate provides several helper functions to convert from some standard formats, that are fairly robust to different sub conventions like delimeters or padding.

today1 = ymd("2025-August-11")
today2 = dmy("11/08/25")
today3 = mdy("8.11.2025")
c(today1, today2, today3)

[1] "2025-08-11" "2025-08-11" "2025-08-11"


R has correctly inferred the date in all three cases. We can also use the as.Date function to customise parsing further, by providing a format string to describe how the date string is expected to be formatted. For more information on formatting see the as.Date documentation.
Note that while the dates are printed as strings, they do in fact have a date type:

class(today1)

[1] "Date"


For the Excel date example, if we read Excel files with readxl there won’t be a problem. But, sometimes Excel dates make their way into other file formats, and we can use the janitor package to load them.

student_data$date_of_birth = excel_numeric_to_date(student_data$date_of_birth)
student_data$date_of_birth

 [1] "2001-11-10" "2003-08-12" "2002-09-06" "2003-04-06" "2002-05-11"
 [6] "2004-08-19" "2004-06-08" "2002-12-06" "2004-06-29" "2002-11-30"
[11] "2002-08-04" "2003-07-01" "2002-01-27" "2003-08-19" "2003-10-06"
[16] "2003-09-01" "2004-06-24" "2003-09-06" "2002-01-26" "2002-08-13"




5.3.2 Date Processing
Once dates are in the proper format, there exist various functions to process them. For example, we can extract the year, month or day:

c(year(today()), month(today()), day(today()))

[1] 2026   10   16


For example, if we want to compute a student’s age we can use lubridate’s interval function followed by time_length

student_data$age = interval(student_data$date_of_birth, today()) |>
    time_length("years")
student_data$age

 [1] 24.93151 23.17808 24.10959 23.52877 24.43288 22.15890 22.35616 23.86027
 [9] 22.29863 23.87671 24.20000 23.29315 24.71781 23.15890 23.02740 23.12329
[17] 22.31233 23.10959 24.72055 24.17534

student_data$age |> floor()

 [1] 24 23 24 23 24 22 22 23 22 23 24 23 24 23 23 23 22 23 24 24


Or, we could use as.period to get a precise calendar difference:

interval(student_data$date_of_birth, today()) |>
    as.period(unit="years")

 [1] "24y 11m 6d 0H 0M 0S"  "23y 2m 4d 0H 0M 0S"   "24y 1m 10d 0H 0M 0S" 
 [4] "23y 6m 10d 0H 0M 0S"  "24y 5m 5d 0H 0M 0S"   "22y 1m 27d 0H 0M 0S" 
 [7] "22y 4m 8d 0H 0M 0S"   "23y 10m 10d 0H 0M 0S" "22y 3m 17d 0H 0M 0S" 
[10] "23y 10m 16d 0H 0M 0S" "24y 2m 12d 0H 0M 0S"  "23y 3m 15d 0H 0M 0S" 
[13] "24y 8m 19d 0H 0M 0S"  "23y 1m 27d 0H 0M 0S"  "23y 0m 10d 0H 0M 0S" 
[16] "23y 1m 15d 0H 0M 0S"  "22y 3m 22d 0H 0M 0S"  "23y 1m 10d 0H 0M 0S" 
[19] "24y 8m 20d 0H 0M 0S"  "24y 2m 3d 0H 0M 0S"  


We could also just subtract the dates, but this gives a difference in terms of days which would be difficult to convert to years (due to leap years).

today() - student_data$date_of_birth

Time differences in days
 [1] 9106 8466 8806 8594 8924 8093 8165 8715 8144 8721 8839 8508 9028 8459 8411
[16] 8446 8149 8441 9029 8830




5.3.3 Times and Time Zones
Times can be handled similarly to dates. There are routines for loading times that are similar to the date-specific routines described above:

time1 = ymd_hms("2025-08-11 11:33:01")
time1

[1] "2025-08-11 11:33:01 UTC"

time2 = now()
time2

[1] "2026-10-16 16:11:50 BST"


We can then extract hours, minutes and seconds:

c(hour(time1), minute(time1), second(time1))

[1] 11 33  1


One extra consideration with times is the time zone. For example, we can see that the time zone of time1 and time2 differ, above:

c(tz(time1), tz(time2))

[1] "UTC" ""   


Note that tz(time2) returns an empty string, which is standard in R for the current time zone. If we want to be explicit we can force now to be in a particular time zone, e.g.

time3 = now("Asia/Tokyo")
tz(time3)

[1] "Asia/Tokyo"


We can also change the time zone on times using the with_tz function:

with_tz(time1, "Asia/Tokyo")

[1] "2025-08-11 20:33:01 JST"

time1

[1] "2025-08-11 11:33:01 UTC"


Notice that this adjusts the time from the previous time zone (UTC) to match the new time zone (JST). If we want to add a time zone without changing the time, we use the force_tz function:

force_tz(time1, "Asia/Tokyo")

[1] "2025-08-11 11:33:01 JST"


Now the time is the same as time1, but the time zone has been modified.


5.3.4 Formatting Dates and Times
By default invoking today1 in R uses the specific format 2025-08-11. We may wish to use another format, for which we can invoke the format function. This takes a date and a format string (as per as.Date, above), and outputs a string in that format. For example:

format(today1, "%Y-%m-%d")

[1] "2025-08-11"

format(today1, "%d %b %y")

[1] "11 Aug 25"

format(time1, "%d %b %y %H:%M")

[1] "11 Aug 25 11:33"

title: 6  Data Visualisation Principles
text:
6.1 The Grammar of Graphics Framework
The Grammar of Graphics (Wilkinson 2005) is implemented in R through the library ggplot2, a core library in tidyverse. It provides a systematic approach to constructing data visualisations. Rather than thinking about chart types (bar chart, scatter plot, etc.), the grammar breaks down visualisations into fundamental components that can be combined in flexible ways.

6.1.1 Core Components of the Grammar
The grammar consists of several key layers:
Data: The dataset being visualised. In ggplot2 this is assumed to be in tidy format. Aesthetics: referred to as aes in ggplot2. These are the visual properties that represent data variables, including:

Position (\((x,y)\) coordinates)
Colour (hue, saturation)
Shape (point shapes, line types)
Size (point size, line width)
Transparency (alpha values)

Geometries: the geometric objects that represent data points. How these are referred to in ggplot2 is included in parentheses below.

Points (geom_point())
Lines (geom_line())
Bars (geom_bar(), geom_col())
Areas (geom_area())
Text (geom_text())

Statistics (stat): (optional) statistical transformations applied to data before plotting, e.g.:

Count (frequency tables)
Smoothing (trend lines)
Binning (histograms)

Scales: How aesthetics translate data values to visual properties:

Continuous scales (for numeric data)
Discrete scales (for categorical data)
Colour scales (viridis colour maps, brewer colour palettes)
Position scales (log or square-root transformations)

Coordinate Systems: How data coordinates map to the plane of the plot:

Cartesian coordinates (most common)
Polar coordinates
Map projections

Faceting: Break data into subsets for producing multiple smaller charts:

facet_wrap(): arranges panels in rows and columns
facet_grid(): arranging panels in a grid based on variables.



6.1.2 Constructing Plots by Composing Components
The grammar allows components to be composed with one another by “adding” them to a plot to build visualisations incrementally.

6.1.2.1 Building a Plot Step by Step
Every ggplot2 plot begins with a call to ggplot(), to which we supply the data and an aesthetic mapping (aes) saying which variables should control which visual properties. On its own this sets up the axes but draws nothing, because we have not yet said how the data should be represented:

library(tidyverse)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g))








To actually see the data we add a geometry. Layers are combined with the + operator, and adding geom_point() draws one point per observation:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).















Warningggplot2 uses +, not |>



ggplot2 layers are joined with +, not the pipe |> you met in Section 2.4.2. This is because ggplot2 is older than the pipe. Confusing the two is one of the most common beginner errors.
penguins |>                                       # pipe the data in
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()                                    # add layers with +


We can encode a third variable by mapping it to another aesthetic. Mapping species to colour gives each species its own colour:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Finally, we can add informative labels with labs() and change the overall appearance with a theme:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin flipper length vs body mass",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Each step simply adds another component to the previous plot. (Thinking of it in this way may help you to distinguish from piping in the rest of tidyverse).


6.1.2.2 A Gallery of Examples
The examples below build on this same pattern to produce richer plots, each highlighting a different part of the grammar we listed above; we will go into building them in much more detail in the lab.
Building on the scatter plot above, we can split the data into a separate panel for each island using facet_wrap(~island), a convenient way to compare the same relationship across groups:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~island) +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin measurements by species, faceted by island",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Because geometries are simply layers, we can stack several of them on a single plot. Here we add two geom_smooth trend lines on top of the scatter points: one per species (coloured) and one overall (dashed black). This lets us compare the per-species trends against the overall one. The points use alpha = 0.6 so that overlapping points show through, which is a common way to deal with overplotting:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = species), alpha = 0.6, size = 2) + # scatter points
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = species), method = "lm", se = TRUE) + # trend-line per species
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) + # overall trend line
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Species") + # Species colour scale
  labs(
    title = "Multiple Geometries: Points + Trend Lines",
    subtitle = "Species-specific trends (coloured) vs overall trend (dashed)",
    x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`).
Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`).


Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Some geometries apply a statistical transformation to the data before anything is drawn. A histogram bins the data and counts how many observations fall in each bin (here rescaled to a density), while geom_density fits a smooth estimate of the distribution. Drawing both together shows the same data summarised in two ways. We use one panel per species (with facet_wrap) so that the distributions do not overlap:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density), fill = species),
                 bins = 30) + # histogram of densities (rather than counts)
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) + # smooth density estimate
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Species") +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Transformations: Histogram + Density",
    x = "Body Mass (g)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).


Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_density()`).









Scales control how data values map to visual properties, and can apply transformations of their own. Here both axes and the colour scale use a base-10 logarithmic transform. Two further aesthetics, colour (body mass) and size (flipper length), are mapped on top of the \(x\) and \(y\) positions, so the plot shows four variables at once:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = body_mass_g, size = flipper_length_mm), alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Body Mass (g)", transform = "log10") +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Flipper Length (mm)", range = c(1, 8)) +
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log10") +
  scale_y_continuous(transform = "log10") +
  labs(
    title = "Scale Transformations: Log Scales",
    subtitle = "Both axes and colour scale transformed",
    x = "Bill Length (mm) - Log Scale",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm) - Log Scale"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









A common use of composition is to overlay a summary on top of the raw distribution. Here we combine a violin plot (which shows the shape of the distribution) with a narrow boxplot (which shows the median and quartiles):

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) +                        # distribution shape
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA) +  # median and quartiles on top
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Species") +
  labs(
    title = "Composing Geometries: Violin + Boxplot",
    subtitle = "Distribution shape (violin) with median and quartiles (boxplot)",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_ydensity()`).


Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).















TipExtending ggplot2



Everything above uses ggplot2 itself, but one of its great strengths is that it can be extended by other packages that add new geometries, scales and facets. A few popular examples are ggforce (extra geometries such as sina plots and zoomed facets), patchwork (for combining several separate plots into one figure), and gganimate (for animated plots). These need to be installed separately (e.g. install.packages("ggforce")) and loaded with library() before use. A browsable catalogue is available at the ggplot2 extensions gallery.

section: 6.2 Common Chart Types and When to Use Them
text:
6.2 Common Chart Types and When to Use Them
The grammar lets you build almost any plot, but in practice a handful of chart types cover most situations. A good starting point is to ask what kind of question you are trying to answer:








Question
Typical chart
Key geometry




How does a numeric value compare across categories?
Bar chart
geom_bar() / geom_col()


How is a single numeric variable distributed?
Histogram, boxplot or violin
geom_histogram(), geom_boxplot()


How are two numeric variables related?
Scatter plot
geom_point()


How does a value change over time (or another ordered variable)?
Line chart
geom_line()



We have already met scatter plots and histograms above; here are the other staples.

6.2.1 Bar Charts: geom_bar() vs geom_col()
There are two bar-chart geometries, and confusing them is a common source of frustration.
geom_bar() counts the rows in each category for you (it applies the count statistic). Use it when you want the frequency of raw observations, for example how many penguins there are of each species:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Number of penguins per species", x = "Species", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()








geom_col(), by contrast, expects you to have already computed the height of each bar, and draws bars of exactly that height (it uses the identity statistic). Use it when your data already contains the values you want to plot, for example a mean you have calculated with dplyr:

penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = mean_mass)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Mean body mass per species", x = "Species", y = "Mean body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal()








In short: reach for geom_bar() to count rows, and geom_col() when you already have the numbers.


6.2.2 Boxplots
A boxplot summarises a numeric variable across categories, showing the median, the interquartile range (the box) and the spread (the whiskers), along with any outliers:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Body mass by species", x = "Species", y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).









Boxplots are compact and good for comparing many groups, but they hide the underlying shape of the data (for example, whether it has two peaks). That is why overlaying the raw distribution, as in the violin and boxplot example above, can be useful.


6.2.3 Line Charts
A line chart connects observations in order along the \(x\)-axis, which makes it the natural choice for showing change over time. Here we use the gapminder dataset from Week 4 to plot life expectancy over time for three countries:

library(gapminder)
gapminder |>
  filter(country %in% c("United Kingdom", "Japan", "Korea, Rep.")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Country") +
  labs(title = "Life expectancy over time", x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_minimal()








Because the line joins successive years, trends and crossovers are easy to spot: Japan overtakes the United Kingdom in the late 1960s, while South Korea rises steeply and has almost caught up by 2007. Note that South Korea is recorded as "Korea, Rep." in gapminder; it is always worth checking how values are spelled in the data before filtering on them.

title: 6  Data Visualisation Principles
text:
6.3 Visual Perception and Plot Interpretation
So far we have concentrated on how to build a plot. But being able to draw a figure is not the same as drawing a good one. ggplot gives us a lot of freedom to design our figures, and it does not tell us which designs are clear and which are misleading. For example, this plot gives the impression that welfare recipients in the US are spiralling out of control - but the \(y\)-axis starts from 94,000,000:



Plot of Federal Welfare Recipients in the USA, from here


The next example was presented by General H.R. McMaster to US officials in 2009, intended to explain the complexity of US military strategy in Afghanistan. It led the New York Times to publish an article called We Have Met the Enemy, and He Is Powerpoint.



We Have Met the Enemy, and He Is Powerpoint, from here.


Careful thought is needed to ensure that plots effectively convey the information that we want them to convey.

6.3.1 Perceptual Accuracy of Visual Elements
(Cleveland and McGill 1984) developed a theory of graphical perception, the process by which people decode quantitative information from visual representations. They argue that the effectiveness of a graph depends on how accurately viewers can visually judge the data or information that the graph encodes. They rank elementary perceptual tasks, like judging position along a common scale, length, area, angle, colour etc. by how precisely humans can perform them, based on controlled experiments.
They found that:

Position along a common scale is judged most accurately,
Length, angle and slope are less accurate, with angle and slope worse than length,
Area, volume or colour saturation are even less reliable.

These provide guidance for how we should encode data into graphs. For example, bar charts (measuring length), aligned on a common scale (height) might be preferred to pie charts (comparing angle and area).
Since (Cleveland and McGill 1984), visualisation theory has continued to develop. The full theory is well beyond the scope of this course, but the main points are:

Not all visual encodings are equal. As (Cleveland and McGill 1984) shows, position can be read most accurately, then length/angle, then area/colour.
Design with perception in mind. Prioritise encodings that make the main comparison easier, using the most informative visual encoding.
Modern tools help. ggplot2 is based on the (Wilkinson 2005), which builds on these ideas. The mapping of aes to geoms describe these perceptual choices.



6.3.2 Colour Blindness Considerations
Another important concern is accessibility. Around 8% of men and 0.5% of women are affected by colour blindness, which can make some plots impossible to perceive for some users. It is also worthwhile to be mindful that your plots may be printed out in black-and-white or viewed on greyscale screens, so relying solely on colour to make points is better avoided.
The most common type of colour blindness is red-green deficiencies, so using red-green contrast should be avoided. Fortunately, ggplot makes it straightforward to adhere to this by providing perceptually uniform, colourblind-safe palettes such as viridis or the ColorBrewer safe sets. Where possible it is still best to make sure there is visual redundancy, rather than using colour alone, using label, shape or line type.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("Adelie" = "red", "Chinstrap" = "green", "Gentoo" = "blue")) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









It would be difficult for someone with red-green colour blindness to distinguish Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species, shape=species)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  scale_colour_brewer(type="qual") +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Using scale_colour_brewer with type="qual" tells R that this is qualitative data (as opposed to sequential, where the factor ordering is meaningful); an appropriate colour palette is then selected automatically. The addition of shape=species also ensures that a viewer who finds colour perception challenging will still be able to interpret the plot.


6.3.3 Principles for Honest and Effective Visualisation
ggplot2 will happily draw whatever you ask of it, so the responsibility for making a plot clear and honest rests with you. The following principles draw together the ideas above into a checklist you can use both to design a visualisation and to critique one:

Be honest with scales. Choose axis limits that represent the data fairly. The welfare chart above is misleading precisely because its \(y\)-axis starts at 94,000,000, exaggerating a small relative change; for bar charts in particular, the value axis should usually start at zero.
Choose the encoding that makes the key comparison accurate. Following (Cleveland and McGill 1984), prefer position and length over angle, area or colour for the comparison that matters most. This is why a bar chart is usually clearer than a pie chart.
Reduce clutter. Every element should earn its place. The Afghanistan strategy diagram fails because it drowns the viewer in detail. When points overlap heavily (overplotting), transparency (the alpha setting used in several plots above) or jittering can reveal the underlying density.
Label directly and informatively. Use labs() to give the plot a meaningful title and clearly labelled axes, with units where relevant, so the figure can be understood without external explanation.
Design for accessibility. Use colourblind-safe palettes such as viridis, and add redundant encodings (shape, line type or direct labels) so the plot does not rely on colour alone.

It is worth running through this list whenever you make a plot, asking of each choice whether it helps or hinders the reader.




Cleveland, William S., and Robert McGill. 1984. “Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 79 (387): 531–54. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478080.


Wilkinson, Leland. 2005. The Grammar of Graphics. Springer-Verlag. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28695-0.

title: 7  SQL for Data Science
text:
7.1 What is a Relational Database?
A relational database is a structured collection of data organized into tables (also called relations). Each table consists of rows (records) and columns (fields), where each column has a specific data type and each row represents a single entry.
To draw analogies with data frames, each table is essentially a data frame. However, the data frames are linked through a key mechanism. Each table has a column that is referred to as a primary key which is like a unique identifier for the row. Often this is an integer, but it can be other things (e.g. a string, or a UUID). The important thing is that each value of a primary key can exist only once in the table, to ensure the row can be identified uniquely.
A table can also have foreign keys: columns whose values refer to primary keys in other tables, thus allowing for relations between the tables. If a column is labelled as a foreign key, consistency checks will be performed to ensure that the foreign key exists in the table it refers to.

7.1.1 Why use Relational Databases?
Relational databases offer several advantages:

Data Integrity: Enforce rules (such as primary and foreign keys) to maintain accurate and consistent data.
Scalability: Efficiently handle large volumes of data and complex queries.
Flexibility: Support powerful querying and data manipulation using SQL.
Security: Provide robust access controls and user permissions.
Redundancy Reduction: Minimize data duplication through normalization (i.e. breaking down the data into smaller, related tables rather than a single large table).
Concurrent Access: Allow multiple users to access and modify data safely at the same time.
Backup and Recovery: Offer built-in mechanisms for data backup and restoration.

title: 7  SQL for Data Science
text:
7.2 What is SQL?
SQL (Structured Query Language) is a standardized language used to manage and manipulate relational databases. It allows users to define, query, update, and control access to data stored in tables. SQL is declarative, meaning you specify what data you want, not how to retrieve it. Common SQL operations include selecting data (SELECT), filtering (WHERE), joining tables (JOIN), aggregating results (GROUP BY), and modifying data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). SQL is widely supported by database systems such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, and Microsoft SQL Server, though there are some features that differ between implementations. In this course we will focus on sqlite, since it is widely available and does not require access to a server on which to host the database.






NoteUsing SQLite



In this chapter we describe how relational databases behave in general, as provided by database servers such as PostgreSQL or MySQL. SQLite supports all of the SQL in this chapter, but it is a deliberately lightweight system, and its behaviour differs from that of a database server in some places — for example, in how strictly it enforces some of the rules described here. More generally, every database system has its own dialect of SQL, so it is worth checking the documentation of the system you are using.








ImportantReading, not writing, SQL



In this course you will not be expected to write SQL yourself. You should, however, be able to read SQL: to interpret a query you are given, and explain what it does and what it returns (Section 7.2.5 gives a guide to doing this). When we work with databases from R, we will write dplyr code and let the dbplyr package translate it into SQL for us (see Section 7.3.1).


Much like R, SQL is typically written in plain text into text files, with the extension .sql. SQL is also stricter on formatting: a script containing several statements must separate them with semicolons (;), and it is good practice to end every statement with one.

7.2.1 Creating a SQLite DB
In this course you will mostly be supplied with pre-built SQLite databases to work with. There are various ways to create a database from scratch. One user-friendly way is using the DB Browser for SQLite. This gives the facility to create new databases and execute arbitrary SQL scripts on them, as well as interactive ways to create tables and insert data.


7.2.2 Creating Tables
The command for creating a table in a database is
    CREATE TABLE <table_name> (
        column_1 <column_1_type>,
        column_2 <column_2_type>, 
        ...,
        <constraints>
    )
It is idiomatic for keywords (e.g. CREATE TABLE) to be in all caps. Unlike R, the column types must be specified when the table is created, and the database checks that the values inserted into each column match its type.
The types that can be used vary between database systems, but most provide at least the following (sometimes under slightly different names):

INTEGER: a whole number.
REAL: a decimal number (called DOUBLE PRECISION or FLOAT in some systems).
TEXT: a text string (often VARCHAR).
BOOLEAN: true or false.
DATE and TIMESTAMP: dates, and dates with times.
BLOB: binary data (we won’t use these).

The examples in this chapter use only INTEGER, REAL and TEXT.
In addition to the type, a column can be designated as the table’s PRIMARY KEY, indicating that it contains the unique identifier for each row. A table has at most one primary key, but it can span several columns, when it is the combination of their values that identifies each row; this is written as a constraint, PRIMARY KEY (column_1, column_2), after the column definitions. We can further add the text AUTOINCREMENT after PRIMARY KEY to have the database generate new IDs automatically; this avoids having to check what the largest ID in a table is before inserting. (The keyword for this is one of the places where database systems differ: SQLite uses AUTOINCREMENT, while for example MySQL uses AUTO_INCREMENT.)
In addition to types, tables can also have constraints. Examples of constraints include:

UNIQUE: the column is not a primary key but each row can only contain unique values.
FOREIGN KEY: the column references the primary key in another table. The syntax for this differs, as we’ll see next.

The SQL examples in the rest of this section are run, in order, against a small SQLite database, so that you can see the result of each query beneath it.
Here is an example that creates three tables, each with a primary key: customers, products, and orders, which links the other two together through foreign keys.

-- Unlike R, comments in SQL start with two hyphens
-- Create customers table
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, 
    first_name TEXT,
    last_name TEXT,
    email TEXT
);


-- Create products table
CREATE TABLE products (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    product_name TEXT,
    price REAL,
    stock INTEGER
);


-- Create orders table
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    customer_id INTEGER,
    product_id INTEGER,
    quantity INTEGER,
    -- Constrain with two foreign keys:
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id)
);

Notice that the customers table holds personal data: names and email addresses. In a real database, data like this is subject to data protection law such as UK GDPR, which limits who may access it and what it may be used for (see Data Ethics); the access controls of a database server are one way of enforcing those limits.






WarningDropping Tables



We can also remove tables using the DROP TABLE syntax. This will delete all the data in the table, so should be used with care! A helpful command is DROP TABLE IF EXISTS which will drop the table only if it exists, otherwise do nothing.




7.2.3 Create, Read, Update and Delete
Once the table structure has been initialised, the four basic operations of persistent storage are Create, Read, Update and Delete (often abbreviated as CRUD).

7.2.3.1 Create
Inserting records into a table is accomplished with the INSERT command.

-- Insert data into customers table
-- Specifying the column names we want to insert into is good practice,

Updating records is accomplished with the UPDATE command:

-- Update the price of a product

7.2.4 Advanced Queries
Beyond reading, filtering and joining tables, SQL has some more advanced syntax that is useful for particular kinds of query.

7.2.4.1 Aggregation
We can perform aggregation using the GROUP BY statement, which is the analogue of group_by in dplyr. This allows us to lump multiple records into a group and specify how they should be aggregated. Some example statements are given below. The first counts the total number of orders for each customer.

-- Count orders per customer

-- Total revenue per product
SELECT product_id, product_name, SUM(quantity * price) AS total_revenue
FROM orders

Notice that product_name appears in the GROUP BY as well as product_id: every column in the SELECT must either be grouped by, or be calculated by an aggregate function such as SUM or COUNT. (Here each product_id has a single product_name, so grouping by both gives the same groups as grouping by product_id alone.)


7.2.4.2 Subqueries
Sometimes we might not be able to compute a table of interest using a single query; we might need to perform two queries to accomplish this. For example, if we want to view the details of customers who have placed more than one order, we first need to execute a query on the orders table to identify those customers, then filter the customers table based on the IDs. To accomplish this we can use subqueries, to nest the orders query inside another query.

-- Find customers who have placed more than one order
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM customers
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

FROM products

Missing values are represented in SQL by NULL, the equivalent of NA in R (see Week 2). Like NA, NULL means “unknown”, so any comparison with it is also unknown: a condition such as email = NULL is never true, and a WHERE clause using it keeps no rows at all. To test whether a value is missing, use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL instead:

-- customers with no email address recorded
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM customers
WHERE email IS NULL;

Aggregate functions such as SUM and AVG skip NULLs, as if na.rm = TRUE had been set in R; so does COUNT(column_name), whereas COUNT(*) counts every row.



7.2.5 Reading SQL Queries
You will have noticed that most SQL clauses have a direct counterpart in dplyr, which we met in Week 4 and 5:

The main difference is in the order of the steps. A dplyr pipeline is written in the order in which it runs, from top to bottom. A SQL query is always written in the same fixed order, beginning with SELECT, but the database evaluates its clauses in a different order:

FROM and JOIN: assemble the rows from the tables.
WHERE: keep only the rows that satisfy the condition.
GROUP BY: split the remaining rows into groups.
HAVING: keep only the groups that satisfy the condition.
SELECT: compute the columns of the result, including aggregates such as COUNT(*).
DISTINCT: remove duplicate rows.
ORDER BY: sort the result.
LIMIT: keep only the first few rows.

To read a query, therefore, start at FROM rather than at SELECT. For example, this query
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
WHERE quantity >= 2
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 5;
reads, in evaluation order: take the orders table; keep the orders of at least two items; group them by customer; keep the customers with more than one such order; for each, report the customer’s ID and their number of orders; sort with the most orders first; and keep the top five. In dplyr, the same steps appear in the same order:
orders |>
    filter(quantity >= 2) |>
    group_by(customer_id) |>
    summarise(order_count = n()) |>
    filter(order_count > 1) |>
    arrange(desc(order_count)) |>
    head(5)
The evaluation order also explains some of SQL’s rules. WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped, so it cannot refer to aggregates such as COUNT(*); that is the job of HAVING, which filters the groups afterwards. Similarly, in most databases a name defined with AS in the SELECT can be used in ORDER BY, which comes later, but not in WHERE, which comes earlier.
dbplyr, which we meet below, does this translation in the other direction: it turns a dplyr pipeline into SQL, which we can read using the same approach.

title: 7  SQL for Data Science
text:
7.3 Why Use SQL vs. R
You will by now have noticed that SQL can do much of what we learned to do with dplyr in Weeks 4–5 (see Section 7.2.5). We discussed the advantages of a database for storing data in Section 7.1.1. This section is about a different question: once the data are stored in a database, where should the work of filtering, joining and summarising them be done? There are two options:

run the query in the database, and import only its result into R; or
import the tables into R, and run the query there using dplyr.

Doing the work in the database has several advantages:

Less data to transfer. Only the result of the query leaves the database. A summary of a table with millions of rows might be a handful of rows, so moving it to R is far quicker than moving the table itself, particularly when the database is on a remote server.
Data larger than memory. R holds the data it works on in memory, whereas a database works with data stored on disk, so it can process tables far too large to load into R at all. In Week 10 we will meet DuckDB, a database designed for analysing large datasets, which can even run queries directly on CSV files stored on disk, using the same dplyr verbs.
Speed. Databases are designed for exactly these operations. They plan how to carry out each query efficiently, can use indexes to find matching rows without reading the whole table, and often run on a server more powerful than your own computer.
Privacy. If only summaries leave the database, sensitive individual-level data, such as the names and email addresses in our example, never need to be copied onto your computer. Combined with the access controls of a database server, this can make it much easier to handle personal data responsibly (see Data Ethics).

Doing the work in R has advantages too:

Expressiveness. R can do far more than SQL: statistical modelling, visualisation, and the many functions provided by R packages. As we will see in Section 7.3.1, only some R functions can be translated into SQL.
Simplicity for small data. If a table fits comfortably in memory, it is often simpler to import it once and work with it in R, rather than querying the database again for every change to the analysis.

In practice, the two are usually combined: the database does the filtering, joining and summarising that reduce the data to what the analysis needs, and R does the rest. Whichever you choose, the query is part of your analysis, so it belongs in your code, alongside the rest of the analysis, rather than being run separately by hand: this keeps the whole analysis reproducible (Chapter 3). dbplyr, which we turn to next, makes this especially convenient, because the boundary between the two becomes a single call to collect().

7.3.1 The Bridge: dbplyr
The R library dbplyr allows you to connect to a database and interact with it as though it were dplyr, while still getting SQL level performance. The file data/customers.db contains a larger version of the database above: it has the same three tables, created with the same CREATE TABLE statements, but contains more customers, products and orders, so the results below differ from those of the small examples above. Here’s how we can interact with it using dbplyr.

# additional packages required
# install.packages("DBI")
# install.packages("dbplyr")
# install.packages("RSQLite")

library(dplyr)

# Connect to the SQLite database
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/customers.db")

7.3.1.1 Using dbplyr Well
Because dbplyr translates our code into SQL, rather than running it in R, there are a few things to bear in mind.
Call collect() as late as possible. Everything before collect() runs in the database, and only its result is sent to R; everything after it runs in R, on data that has already been transferred. These two pipelines give the same result:

# filter in the database: only the matching rows are sent to R
orders |> filter(quantity >= 3) |> collect()

# filter in R: the whole table is sent to R first
orders |> collect() |> filter(quantity >= 3)

but the first sends R only the matching orders, while the second transfers the entire orders table before discarding most of it. On a table this small the difference is negligible; on one with millions of rows, it is the difference between a query that finishes in seconds and one that does not fit in memory.
Only functions that dbplyr knows how to translate can be used before collect(). dbplyr translates common functions, such as the arithmetic operators, mean(), n() and paste(), into their SQL equivalents. Functions without an equivalent in the database’s SQL cannot be translated, and cause an error:

customers |>
    mutate(padded_name = stringr::str_pad(first_name, 10)) |>
    collect()

Error in `stringr::str_pad()`:
! `str_pad()` is not available in this SQL variant.


The fix is to do as much work as possible in the database, then collect() the result and use the function in R afterwards.
A lazy table can only be joined to another table in the same database. Joining it to a tibble that lives in R fails:

vip_customers = tibble(id = c(1, 4), level = c("gold", "silver"))

customers |> inner_join(vip_customers, by = "id")

Error in `auto_copy()`:
! `x` and `y` must share the same src.
i `x` is a <tbl_SQLiteConnection/tbl_dbi/tbl_sql/tbl_lazy/tbl> object.
i `y` is a <tbl_df/tbl/data.frame> object.
i Set `copy = TRUE` if `y` can be copied to the same source as `x` (may be
  slow).


As the error message suggests, adding copy = TRUE copies the tibble into a temporary table in the database, after which the join can run there:

    inner_join(vip_customers, by = "id", copy = TRUE) |>
    collect()

For a small tibble like this one, copying is cheap; for a large one, it may be better to collect() the database table first, if it is small enough, and join in R.
Finally, we close the connection to the database once we have finished with it:

dbDisconnect(con)
